chapter_theme: Kurinji in the time of the secret love: the friend forbids the night path and the field, naming the elephants, the armed kin and the town's gossip (1, 5-8), while the heroine, pale and with loosening bangles, waits for the hill lord to come, until the harvest ends and her mother keeps her from the field (2-4, 9, 10).

1.reading: The friend tells the lord of the sky-high hill, where sandal burnt with a grass fire sends up its smoke as an offering and dust rains down, that he must not come by night, since the dark ways hold elephants.
1.nuance: The opening may make the hill a place of worship: புலவோர் 'who are given smoke' reads most easily as the celestials receiving burnt sandal, so the hill he comes from is sacred and fragrant, and the warning that closes the poem turns that grandeur into danger. The last word கரம் is hard; 'hidden ways' or 'trunks' are both possible.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill and the night visit forbidden fix kurinji and its midnight tryst

2.reading: The friend asks the lord of the mighty hill, where the kaanthal's clustered buds bloom like hands and the female monkey, taking them for fragrant buds, plays with them, whether his coming will now be hard, since the guarding of the millet fields has ended.
2.nuance: The end of the field-watch is the end of the girl's licensed days outdoors, so the question about his coming is a push toward marriage. The monkey's delight in the hand-like buds is an image of the hill's ease set against the closing of their meetings; its exact sense (மணமுகை, fragrant bud or wedding bud) is open.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaanthal, the hill monkey and the millet field are kurinji things

comparisons.tenor: the clustered buds of the kaanthal, shaped like hands

3.reading: The heroine says that the bangles that slipped here are not as they were on the day she joined the lord of the flowered hill, where on the high steep slope the kaanthal blooms and thunder, taking it for a snake, rushes and strikes and roars.
3.nuance: Thunder that kills snakes is a stock hill image; here it falls on a flower that only looks like a snake's hood, so the violence lands on something harmless. Set beside the loosened bangles it reads as the hurt that has come to her though she did no wrong, but there is no act of a person in it and it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the kaanthal on the hill slope and the hill lord

comparisons.tenor: the kaanthal blossom, which the thunder takes for a snake's hood

4.reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the lord of the sky-high hill will come, so that the pallor of her body may leave, in his hill where the hunters' children pick up the wet gems lying in the millet field and warm their hands at them by night as if at embers.
4.nuance: Gems so common that children use them as a fire make the hill rich beyond need, which sharpens the one thing she lacks: his coming, the only cure she names for her pallor.

thinai_evidence.note: the millet field and the hill hunters' children

comparisons.tenor: the glowing gems, at which the children warm their hands as at embers

5.reading: The friend tells the man not to come among the hills, for those who guard the ripening fields on the fragrant slope are her kin, harsh of word, with bows, spears and swift arrows, living among the rocks.
5.nuance: The threat is built as a list of weapons, and the last word, எமர் 'our people', is held back to the end, so the danger is named as kinship: the men he would face are the girl's own family, whose consent marriage would need.

thinai_evidence.note: the field-guards and bowmen of the rocky hill are kurinji people

6.reading: The friend tells the man that they are daughters of the hill folk who live in the forest of the long gem-bright hill where elephants roam, and asks why he comes into the millet field, since their kin would rage even to see him.
6.nuance: The friend's 'we' names the two girls by their tribe, so the refusal speaks in the voice of the family; it is the same self-naming the friend uses in verse 8 to turn aside his pretext.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill folk's daughters in the millet field of the elephant hill

7.reading: The friend tells the lord of the good land of the mighty hill, whose falling cascades sound as lute, flute and drum together, that the girl with a young deer's glance cannot bear his absence, but that if he comes by night it will bring gossip the whole town knows.
7.nuance: The waterfall as an orchestra makes the hill a stage, and the warning follows from it: what happens on a stage is heard, and the night visit will become the town's talk. The girl's distress is set against the danger, which leaves marriage as the only way out.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill cascade and the night visit

comparisons.tenor: the sound of the falling cascade, like lute, flute and drum in concert
the girl, whose glance is a young deer's

8.reading: The friend answers the man who asks after a wounded elephant: we are girls of the hill folk with soft shoulders like bending bamboo, on this cool slope fragrant with blooming vengai, and no tusker came this way, sir, flagging and streaming blood.
8.nuance: His question is the hunter's pretext for speaking to the girls, and the friend answers it literally, which is a way of showing she sees through it; she also names who they are, the hill folk's daughters, as in verse 6.

thinai_evidence.note: the vengai slope, the hill girls and the hunted tusker

comparisons.tenor: the girls' soft shoulders, like bending bamboo

9.reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the lord of the gem hill will come, so that her sickly colour leaves and her broad bamboo shoulders fill out again, in this lovely evening when the vengai, the tree that tells the season, is in full flower and bees hum.
9.nuance: கணி, 'the reckoner', is a name of the vengai, whose flowering marks the season of the millet harvest and of weddings; so the evening she describes is a sign that the time for his coming to marry her is here.

thinai_evidence.note: the flowering vengai and the hill lord

iraicchi.act: the male monkey that has got a jackfruit calls its mate to share it
iraicchi.sense: the hill lord, who has the means, should likewise call her to him openly, now that the field where they met is closed to her

10.reading: The heroine asks her friend whether the lord of the rock-ringed hill, where the green-eyed male monkey that has got a jackfruit calls its mate with 'ela!', will be vexed, now that mother, learning of their union, has forbidden her to go to the millet field.
10.nuance: The confinement (இற்செறிப்பு) ends the field meetings; the question whether he will be vexed is put so that he, or the friend for him, will see that only marriage can bring them together again.

thinai_evidence.note: the jackfruit, the hill monkey and the millet field

links.note: Both are the friend forbidding the night visit by a path where elephants go; Akananuru 318 adds 'மன்றல் வேண்டினும் பெறுகுவை', you may have the wedding if you want it.
links.teaches: The four-line verse stops at the prohibition, and the long poem shows what the prohibition is for: shutting the night road is the friend's way of pressing for marriage, which Thinaimozhi 1 leaves unsaid.

links.note: Akananuru 28 warns that the millet ears are bowing and stalks are showing, so the girl may soon be replaced at the field; Thinaimozhi 2 says the guarding of the fields has ended.
links.teaches: Read in order the two poems give the harvest as the clock of the secret love, a warning while the ears ripen and the closed field once they are cut, so the end of the field-watch is the end of their meetings.

links.note: In Akananuru 28 the mother would replace the girl at the field if she failed to scare the parrots; in Thinaimozhi 10 the mother bars her from the field because she has learnt of the union.
links.teaches: The pair shows two routes to the same confinement, neglect of the field-watch and the mother's knowledge, which makes clear that the millet field is the one place the girl is allowed out, and losing it is losing him.

links.note: Both answer the man with the same self-naming, குறவர் மகளிரேம், we are daughters of the hill folk; 6 adds that their kin would rage, 8 that no wounded tusker came this way.
links.teaches: The repeated formula works as a fence: in 6 it states the kin's threat outright, and in 8 the same words deflect his hunting pretext, showing that naming the tribe is itself the friend's refusal.

links.note: Akananuru 82 makes the hill a stage where the waterfall is the drum, the bamboo wind the flute and the bees the lute, with a peacock dancing; Thinaimozhi 7 compresses it to one line, the cascade sounding as lute, flute and drum.
links.teaches: In both the orchestra of the hill sets up an audience: in Akananuru 82 many saw him at the field, and in Thinaimozhi 7 the night visit will be known to the whole town, so the stage image carries the danger of the love being seen and heard.

links.note: Thinaimozhi 7 uses ஊரறி கௌவை, gossip the town knows, as the harm that a night visit will bring; Kural 1143 has the man welcome the ஊரறிந்த கெளவை as a foretaste of having her. On a plain reading the town's gossip is a threat in one and a gain in the other.
links.teaches: The same phrase is a warning in the friend's mouth and a prize in the lover's, so the Kural's couplet reads as his reply to exactly the argument the friend uses to keep him away.

links.note: In Akananuru 388 the young hunter asks the girls on the millet platform whether a tusker wounded by his arrow has passed by their field; in Thinaimozhi 8 the friend answers that no bleeding tusker came this way.
links.teaches: The long poem gives the pretext question and the short one gives only the reply, which a reader can only read as a reply because the question is a fixed form; together they show the wounded-elephant question as a standard opening the girls know how to parry.

links.note: Both are the woman saying that his coming will take the pallor from her shoulders: Kural 1265, after she has seen her husband with full eyes; Thinaimozhi 9, if the hill lord comes in this vengai evening.
links.teaches: The Kural states the cure as a rule in the wife's mouth, while the earlier stage in Thinaimozhi ties it to the flowering vengai, the season sign of weddings, so the coming that cures the pallor is, before marriage, the wedding itself.

source_issues: 1-10: the core records carry no colophon thurai, so thurai_akam speaker, addressee and stage are inferred from the poems and occasion.words is null throughout.

1 line 4: கரம் is obscure at the close; it may be the elephant's trunk or a word for hidden places, and the sense of the line (the night way holds elephants) does not turn on it. Line 2 புலவோர் is read as the celestials who receive the smoke.
2 line 3: வரிஅரிதாங் is unclear; வரவு அரிது ஆம் ('will coming be hard?') fits the sense and the closing of the field-watch.
7 line 4: flagged as differing from the site, and ௌ repaired from the split encoding; ஊரறி கௌவை reads well as it stands.
9 line 2: தோழ is a masculine vocative in a heroine's speech to her friend; தோழி is probably meant.
